pages.x: In 1931 Japanese officers blew up a stretch of their own railway near Mukden, blamed Chinese soldiers, and used it as an excuse to seize all of Manchuria. Japan set up a puppet state there called Manchukuo, with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, at its head, and walked out of the League of Nations when it objected.

On 7 July 1937 Japanese and Chinese troops exchanged fire at the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beijing, and this time Chiang Kai-shek decided to fight. Japan poured in troops. In Shanghai Chinese armies held out through three months of street fighting before they broke.

In December 1937 Japanese troops took Nanjing, then China's capital, and for six weeks murdered prisoners and civilians and raped tens of thousands of women. A few foreigners set up a safety zone that sheltered some 200,000 people. The number killed is still argued over; China puts it at 300,000.
pages.of: of killing and rape in Nanjing

pages.x: Chiang moved his government far up the Yangtze to Chongqing, behind the mountains, and traded space for time. In 1938 his armies broke the dikes of the Yellow River to stop the Japanese; the flood drowned or starved hundreds of thousands of Chinese farmers. Japanese bombers raided Chongqing again and again.

With its coast in Japanese hands, China was supplied by a mountain road from Burma, built largely by hand by some 200,000 workers. When Japan cut it in 1942, American planes flew supplies over the Himalayas, a route pilots called the Hump, and American volunteer pilots, the Flying Tigers, fought Japanese bombers.

When Japan attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor in December 1941, China's war became part of the Second World War, and a huge part of Japan's army stayed tied down in China to the end. Japan surrendered in August 1945, after the atomic bombs and a Soviet invasion of Manchuria.

The war devastated China, leaving perhaps 15 to 20 million Chinese dead and tens of millions homeless. It weakened Chiang's government and helped the Communists win the civil war that followed. Memories of the war, and of Nanjing above all, still weigh on relations between China and Japan.
